talks.title: Shared-GPU Security Learnings from Fly.io
talks.teaser: Explains how a bare-metal cloud hardens multi-tenant GPU pass-through with VFIO, IOMMU, ACS, ATS controls, and BAR monitoring.
talks.summary:
Matt Braun describes why Fly.io treated customer-accessible data-center GPUs as a remote physical-access threat comparable to Thunderbolt-style DMA attacks, and why Firecracker’s lack of PCIe passthrough pushed the fleet toward cloud-hypervisor with a dual-hypervisor operational cost.

After MIG’s platform limits and vGPU licensing made NVIDIA’s partition models unusable for ephemeral HTTP-driven workloads, the team chose full passthrough via VFIO, leaning on IOMMU groups and IOVA remapping as the primary DMA boundary. The talk walks through BAR layout on host versus guest, MMIO exposure, and hardening options such as eBPF or shimming the VFIO PCI driver when hardware partitioning is unavailable.

Further risks include PCIe peer-to-peer when ACS is missing or misconfigured, ATS allowing devices to embed physical addresses in transaction packets, and unexpected NVLink cabling that bypasses PCIe controls. Firmware on the card (VBIOS, info ROM, GSP drivers supplied from the guest) adds persistence and parsing concerns. Takeaways stress verifying IOMMU grouping and VFIO bindings, disabling ATS when possible, monitoring BARs, fuzzing GPU drivers, and preferring dedicated hardware when shared GPUs are unavoidable.

talks.title: I SPy: Rethinking Entra ID research for new paths to Global Admin
talks.teaser: Traces how Entra ID service principal credentials enable escalation from application admin to Global Admin through first-party apps.
talks.summary:
Entra ID applications are split into two objects: the app registration, which defines the app, and the service principal, which is the identity that acts in a tenant. Credentials on these two objects do not synchronize, so anyone who can add a secret or certificate to a service principal can authenticate as that app in any tenant where it is installed. The talk traces this issue back to 2019, when Microsoft first-party applications were shown to allow privilege escalation, and to later changes that closed some cases but not all.

The research was done directly against Microsoft Graph in a test tenant. Secrets were rejected for many first-party apps, so the work moved to certificates added by patching the service principal, with tokens obtained through the client credentials flow. One app, Office 365 Exchange Online, held a powerful domain permission. Using it, a new domain was added and a federation configuration was set up to trust an attacker-controlled certificate. That allowed forged SAML tokens to target a synchronized user, such as a Global Admin, identified through the on-premises immutable ID, with MFA claims included.

The final twist was that the chain worked from a service principal holding Application Administrator but not from a user with the same role, because only Global Admins could add credentials to that Exchange service principal. Microsoft treated this as an edge case and did not plan a fix. The practical takeaway is to enable the app instance property lock on your own applications and to review credentials on service principals, not only on app registrations, since the portal does not show them the same way.

talks.title: Taming LLMs to Detect Anomalies in Cloud Audit Logs
talks.teaser: Shows how a small language model, trained on cloud audit logs, flags unusual events to cut false positives.
talks.summary:
Cloud environments change constantly, and an administrative action in an audit log can look the same whether a DevOps engineer or an attacker performs it. The talk argues that rule-based detection piles up false positives in this setting. Prompting a general-purpose LLM directly over raw log data helps, but such a model knows nothing about what is normal in one particular environment.

The presenter's method trains a small GPT-2 style model, roughly 100 million parameters, on about 100,000 normalized log records. Each CloudTrail row is reduced to a few fields: zone, event name, source and response code. The model learns which sequences are common, so every token gets a surprise score that can be displayed as a heat map. Rare combinations stand out, such as an access denied response following a list-buckets call from an unusual zone. Training needs no manual labels, and the speaker estimated about an hour on a single GPU.

The flagged events are then added to an off-the-shelf LLM prompt as extra context, which the speaker says gives better triage with fewer false positives than prompting alone. Questions covered why not a classic classifier: the approach needs less machine learning expertise and can be retrained as the environment shifts. For multi-account AWS organizations, the speaker suggested one model per organization, sized somewhat larger than GPT-2.

talks.title: Double Agents: Exposing Hidden Threats in AI Agent Platforms
talks.teaser: Shows how static agent IDs in embedded HTML snippets let outsiders reach supposedly protected AI agents.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at conversational AI agents built on low-code platforms from major cloud providers and smaller vendors, and at how those agents get published on websites. The presenters used Google's Vertex AI agent builder as their main example. An anonymous agent is embedded with an HTML snippet that holds only a project ID and an agent ID, with no token or login flow. They argued that builders often assume an agent is safe because it sits on an internal or authenticated site, but those protections do not apply at the agent level.

The researchers described an attacker workflow. Searching GitHub turned up hundreds of public repositories exposing these snippets. Pasting a snippet into a basic HTML editor was enough to talk to some anonymous agents, which returned internal data within minutes. For search agents, which require an allowed-domain list, they found a domain that kept appearing in the repositories and spoofed it by mapping it to localhost through the hosts file, which got past the check. From there they probed the agent's tools and connected data sources and asked it to share its content. They also noted that attackers could overload agents to cause denial of service or drive up costs.

On disclosure, Google said it does not treat the allowed-domains setting as a security control, and it documents public access as open to anyone, so it did not count the bypass as a vulnerability. The presenters said similar snippet patterns appeared on other platforms, including IBM Watson X and a WordPress AI platform. Their recommendations were to minimise public endpoints, treat agent identifiers as secrets and scan for them, keep a living inventory of agents and the data they touch, and educate users, since non-technical staff can deploy agents in minutes.

talks.title: What Do You Mean, ‘Resource Not Found?’ Demystifying GCP Error Codes for IR & Detections
talks.teaser: Shows how GCP error codes and error details can expose probing and misuse, and how to turn them into detections and response steps.
talks.summary:
Gabriel Freed argues that error responses in Google Cloud audit logs deserve the same attention as successful actions, since they can reveal reconnaissance and misuse before or during an incident. He explains that GCP services use gRPC with the AIP-193 error model, where each error carries a numeric code, an optional message, and a details section with type, domain, and reason, plus error info naming the affected resource. Freed maps these codes to familiar HTTP status equivalents to help analysts read them.

He gives examples of what different errors might mean. Many not-found responses across random bucket names could suggest dictionary-based enumeration, repeated already-exists errors on firewall names could point to an offensive tool reusing names, and a zone resource pool exhausted error could hint at cryptojacking. Permission-denied details can show exactly which permission was missing, and for long-running operations with a null principal, the operation ID can be used to trace back the initiating user.

Three pseudo-code detections follow, covering reconnaissance through resource-not-found bursts, probing across several service accounts for disabled services, and a user checking permissions with a stolen key. Each begins naive and adds context such as user, project, error reason, and thresholds to reduce false positives. The takeaways are to map error codes into fields, baseline callers and their error rates, and stitch operation IDs so no entity is missed.

talks.title: Challenges around AI-as-a-Service logging
talks.teaser: Shows why logs from AI-as-a-service platforms and browsers are inconsistent and hard to centralise for monitoring.
talks.summary:
Jeremy Snyder explains why his team began examining how AI-as-a-service usage gets logged. Generative AI is moving into production quickly, often before security teams know which services and data are involved. He splits AI consumption into workload, meaning applications that call an LLM, and workforce, meaning employees using chat tools, since each produces different logs.

On the server side, the team reviewed Amazon Bedrock logs. They arrived as JSON but varied in metadata, stop sequences and where one interaction ended and the next began. Some models relied on cross-region processing, so data could be handled outside the expected region, a concern for sovereignty requirements. Agent logs also revealed system instructions the team had not written. Guardrail behaviour differed by provider, and one model processed encoded content that a guardrail should have blocked. With no CloudTrail-style service for these logs, centralising them meant routing through S3 or CloudWatch and a Lambda function, multiplied across accounts and regions.

On the client side, browser plugins were the easiest way to capture employee prompts, but endpoint agent logs were often truncated and browsers usually blocked response payloads. The team also found chat interfaces sending file contents before the user clicked submit. He noted log formats changed rapidly and that SaaS AI providers have not yet built audit features for security teams. His advice is to start from the monitoring goals, such as knowing who uses AI and with what data.

talks.title: Logs don't mean a thing: Unraveling IaC-Managed Identity Ownership
talks.teaser: Shows how to find the human owner of cloud identities created by infrastructure-as-code pipelines.
talks.summary:
Owning a non-human identity means being the person who rotates its keys, adjusts its permissions and handles incidents. When infrastructure-as-code creates a cloud role, the activity log names the automation tool instead of a person, and the identity's name is assembled from variables spread across several files. The speakers set out to trace these identities back to the people who change the code.

They compared three approaches. The first clones the code and tags each resource with the file that produced it, which needs no logs but requires executing the IaC engine against environments the team does not control. The second matches a cloud creation event to the CI/CD run whose output contains the same name, then uses the GitHub API to find the pull request author. It works across tools and platforms but is limited by log retention. The third sends code and pipeline files to an LLM, which hallucinated and never produced reliable file links, so it was not finished.

The team picked the log-based method because it required no access to client environments. Q&A added that creation timestamps from the cloud API still help beyond retention windows, that owner tags are awkward when identities have several owners, and that manually kept owner lists go stale. The takeaway: combine several artifacts, keep logs as long as possible, and tag resources in your own environments.

talks.title: Rebuilding ROADRecon for the Modern Entra Environment
talks.teaser: Explains how the Entra enumeration tool Road Recon was rebuilt for Microsoft Graph and what defenders can detect.
talks.summary:
Road Recon is a Python tool that enumerates users, groups, service principals and permissions in an Entra tenant, stores them in an SQLite database and offers a front end for browsing the results. It depends on the Azure AD Graph API, which Microsoft is retiring, so the speaker set out to move it to Microsoft Graph. Microsoft Graph access requires a client that already holds enough preconsented permissions, so the work began by finding first-party applications that could authenticate with the needed scopes through a password grant.

Not every first-party client works in that flow, and some need redirect URLs that are poorly documented. The Microsoft Office client worked best, although conditional access policies can block it, so alternative clients are sometimes needed. Some clients also lack permission to read conditional access or authorization policies. A demo showed the Graph-based version gathering tenant data and displaying it in the interface. The speaker also covered undocumented internal APIs used by the Azure portal, which generate no logs and can be used for enumeration. They are still being mapped, so that route is described as a work in progress and less stable than Graph.

For detection, the default Python user agent is an easy indicator but can be changed. Behavioural analytics on unusual request volumes, attempts across uncommon client and resource pairs, and sign-ins from anomalous network locations may help. Because read-only enumeration is hard to spot, the speaker argued that defenders should focus on sensitive or state-changing actions and collect telemetry across the estate.

talks.title: I Didn’t Register for This: What’s Really in Google’s Artifact Registry?
talks.teaser: Shows how scanning Google-owned container images in Artifact Registry turned up thousands of vulnerabilities and hard-coded secrets.
talks.summary:
The research began when the speaker and a colleague, studying Cloud Composer 3, found a Kubernetes configuration pulling an image from a Google project. Its tags and parent organization ID suggested Google owned and deployed it. A permission gap hid other images in that project, but the legacy gcr.io domain still exposed them, giving a pipeline of discovery, ownership check, pivot and scan.

Images fell into three groups: vetted marketplace images from third parties, offered Google base images, and used images Google runs in its own services. Across more than 3,000 images from 32 repositories, the scan found about 1.7 million vulnerabilities, around 350,000 unique CVEs, and roughly 70,000 unique high or critical ones. Flaws such as Log4Shell, Zerologon and Spring4Shell appeared on several images. One marketplace image had 24 critical findings, nine of them potentially leading to remote code execution. Almost 3,000 secrets turned up, all in the vetted group, including cloud keys, an OpenAI key and hard-coded admin logins.

Google judged the used-category issues non-exploitable or irrelevant, but said it could not assess exploitability for the vetted images. The speaker argues that an upload by Google is not proof of trust, that shared responsibility leaves gaps between vendors and marketplace review, and that users should scan for secrets, use built-in scanning and audit where images come from.

talks.title: Not So Secret: The Hidden Risks of GitHub Actions Secrets
talks.teaser: Shows how GitHub Actions secrets can expose cloud credentials to write-access users, and how environments and OIDC trust rules limit it.
talks.summary:
Many teams keep cloud credentials in GitHub Actions secrets, trusting that repository and organization secrets are well protected. The talk begins with a common pattern: a pipeline that hard-codes credentials is moved to repository secrets, which seem safe because their values cannot be read back in the interface and Actions masks them in logs. A user with write access can create a branch, edit the workflow to print the values in encoded form, and run it. Branch protection on the default branch does not prevent this, because the workflow definition comes from the branch being run and repository secrets are available to every run in that repository.

The next part moves the credentials into a named environment with a protection rule that allows only runs from the main branch. The same modified workflow then fails on a feature branch. The speaker applies the same test to OpenID Connect, where an AWS role trusts any workflow in the repository. Short-lived credentials can still be exported that way, so the fix is to restrict the subject claim to the main branch. When environments are used, the trust policy must reference the environment in the subject, which blocks a run that drops the environment reference.

The takeaways are to assume anyone with write access can read repository secrets, avoid storing them where possible, and use environments as the enforcement point for both static secrets and OIDC roles. Workflow triggers also matter, since their configuration is read from the default branch. Fork-based pull requests, which inject secrets differently, were left out.

talks.title: Putting Workload Identity to Work: Taking SPIFFE past day 0
talks.teaser: Explains how SPIFFE workload identities replace static secrets, and how teams can roll them out at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem SPIFFE addresses: applications and CI pipelines need secrets to authenticate to a vault, which only moves the secret problem one step back. SPIFFE instead issues a short-lived cryptographic identity document to a workload, based on verifiable metadata about it. That metadata can come from an OIDC token in a CI pipeline, a cloud instance's assumed role, a TPM on premises, or Kubernetes pod labels. The document is usually an X.509 certificate carrying a SPIFFE ID, though it can also be a JWT. Workloads use it for mutual TLS and authorization decisions, and SDKs or proxies cover applications that cannot change.

Use cases include replacing workload-to-workload API keys and certificates with continuously rotated credentials, easing the burden of rotating many long-lived database credentials, and restricting traffic by region. One identity can work across AWS, GCP, Azure and on-premises instead of separate key pairs for each cloud. A demo shows a GitHub Actions pipeline receiving a certificate that lasts about as long as the pipeline run. For rollout, the speaker urges choosing one goal, such as developer efficiency, then starting with a tightly scoped use case. One large financial organization began with GitLab CI, then moved services in a multi-tenant data center to workload identity.

Practical advice includes keeping SPIFFE ID structures simple, since adding fields later is easier than removing them, and checking early that the design fits the internal PKI. Lack of native support is a major blocker for legacy databases, where translation proxies are one workaround. Revocation is mostly handled through short certificate lifetimes rather than explicit revocation. The speaker noted that the standard does not define authorization rules, so those remain bespoke. The main takeaways are developer efficiency, reduced breach risk and new capabilities.

talks.title: Inside Microsoft's Battle Against Cloud-Enabled Deepfake Threats
talks.teaser: Shows how stolen cloud AI keys and reverse proxies power deepfake generation, plus Azure-side defenses and runtime logging.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with what deepfakes are and three recent cases: a closed site that sold on-demand synthetic content, a British engineering firm that lost $25 million after a video call impersonated senior management, and a fake video aimed at a candidate in a Slovak election. The presenters report about two years of research into attacks on cloud AI APIs, where deepfake generation was one of the main goals. Attackers obtain cloud credentials through vulnerable applications or secrets left in code repositories, then the compromised account owner pays for the usage.

The middle section covers a reverse proxy used to resell access to stolen keys across several cloud providers, often behind a Cloudflare domain that hides the origin. The speakers link the proxy's developers and sellers to people named in Microsoft's December 2024 lawsuit, and show an earlier attack record that matched those details. They describe D3U, a Python web interface for image generation that can route requests through the proxy. It offers a jailbreak option that wraps prompts to bypass Azure's prompt rewriting, and it strips C2PA content credentials that mark AI-made images.

For defenders, they walk through Microsoft's AI shared responsibility model, where customers own access management, data governance and application design. Recommended controls include role-based access instead of API keys, private networking, image-aware guardrails and runtime monitoring. Because Azure OpenAI does not log model events by default, traffic should pass through API Management and stream diagnostics to an event hub for detection rules, such as watching image generation calls. The talk closes by arguing that content labeling and regulation also need a shared effort.

talks.title: Data Perimeter Implementation Strategies: Lessons Learned Rolling Out SCPs/RCPs
talks.teaser: Walks through rolling out AWS data perimeter SCPs and RCPs at scale, including the policy limits and developer coordination hurdles.
talks.summary:
Vanguard's cloud identity team describes how they defined a data perimeter across hundreds of AWS accounts. They set three boundaries: resource, network and identity. Resource boundaries keep non-production and production apart and block outside resources; network boundaries admit only trusted VPCs and corporate address ranges; identity boundaries admit only trusted internal identities. They applied SCPs and RCPs at account level rather than organizational unit level so exceptions could be tuned per team.

AWS offers no dry-run mode, so the team analysed CloudTrail with Python scripts to find requests that enforcement would break, then sent lists of risky identities and resources to development teams before rollout. Network controls began with privileged identities, and Lambda functions were moved into VPCs under a detective control first. Incomplete CloudTrail logging, and hardcoded VPC IDs and CIDR ranges that pushed policy size toward AWS limits, required workarounds. S3 buckets did not support resource tag conditions, so the team used a coarser principal account condition instead. After rollout, CloudTrail dashboards tracked access-denied spikes, and policies were rolled back when they appeared.

Exceptions were enforced in CI/CD: a policy granting an external account failed the build until a risk was logged and approved, after which a data perimeter tag could be applied. Key takeaways were to start small, win developer buy-in early, focus first on the riskiest identities, design for policy size limits, prefer tag-based approaches, and engineer around unsupported AWS features. In the Q&A, onboarding new accounts was still a manual policy deployment step.

talks.title: ECS-cape - Hijacking IAM Privileges in Amazon ECS
talks.teaser: Shows how a container task can impersonate the ECS agent to steal IAM credentials of other tasks on the same EC2 instance.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how Amazon ECS runs containers on EC2 instances, with each task holding its own IAM task role, and how the ECS agent authenticates to the AWS control plane using the instance role. The speaker found an undocumented websocket channel that the agent uses to receive task credentials, and showed that a single container on the host could reach it and act as the agent.

The attack chain starts with the instance metadata service, which gives any task the instance role credentials. Those credentials are used to call the discover-poll endpoint API, and a container introspection endpoint supplies the identifiers needed to build the websocket request. The request is signed with SigV4 and, once accepted, returns the role credentials of every other task on the same instance. The speaker also noted that the same channel leaks metadata about the instance and other tasks. In a live demo, a task with a deny-everything role used a command-line tool to retrieve an administrator task's credentials and delete an S3 bucket.

For practitioners, the main lesson is that task-level hardening matters on EC2 launch-type ECS. Recommended steps include blocking metadata access for tasks while keeping it for the instance, never granting poll or discover-poll permissions to tasks, separating high- and low-privilege workloads and tenants onto different instances, and keeping task role permissions minimal. The speaker reported that AWS did not treat the issue as a security concern and planned documentation changes, and that AWS feedback pointed to Fargate as not exposed to this path.

talks.title: Patience brings prey: lessons learned from a year of threat hunting in the cloud
talks.teaser: Shows how a year of cloud threat hunting produced new detections, with a compromised-workload case and LLM API abuse findings.
talks.summary:
Greg Foss and Anthony Renzazzo describe the threat hunting program their detection engineering team runs across many customer environments. They separate hunting, which looks for unknown behaviour with a wide net, from threat detection, which codifies known activity, and explain that hunt results feed new detections shipped in their product. Inputs include critical security signals, detection maintenance, a backlog of hypothesis-driven hunts, and quarterly cross-team hunting sessions.

The first case began when tuning a noisy image-download rule exposed a workload compromise. The attacker waited about nine days before deploying a crypto miner and also set up proxyjacking to monetise traffic. The actor had exploited a PHP FastCGI flaw against a Magento site and deployed a rootkit that hid its executables from standard listings. The second case was a hypothesis-driven hunt for LLM API abuse after exposed access keys were seen used against Bedrock. Hunting Azure and Google Cloud turned up little, and the Bedrock query over cloud audit logs produced only two hits, both malicious, which gave indicators to pivot from.

Across the year, the speakers said leaked long-term access keys were the most common route into the cloud management plane, ahead of business email compromise and credential stuffing. Their lessons were to retire hunts that never return results, vary the attack surface to avoid bias, and not dismiss atomic indicators, since much malicious infrastructure stayed unchanged. Findings loop back into detections and AI-assisted workflows that depend on curated, confirmed data.

talks.title: Detecting the Undetectable: Threat Hunting in Appliance Environments
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Detecting the Undetectable: Threat Hunting in Appliance Environments.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Shahar Dorfman and Sagit Sadik, threat researchers from the Wiz research team, present a methodology for threat hunting in virtual appliance environments. Virtual appliances—such as solutions from Ivanti, Aviatrix, and Fortinet—are preconfigured, dedicated software packages where the vendor chooses the OS, application, and dependencies. While simple to deploy, they function as black boxes with immutable file systems, restricted root or SSH access, minimal logging, and strict restrictions preventing administrators from installing conventional telemetry or antivirus agents. Furthermore, appliances frequently run exposed to the internet with high privileges (for example, 65% of monitored Aviatrix instances in AWS held high IAM permissions), making them prime targets: 23% of all known exploited CVEs in enterprise environments were found in appliances.

### Key Topics
- **The Visibility Challenge:** The inability of defenders to run endpoint agents, access files directly, or collect rich host telemetry on appliances.
- **Snapshot Forensics:** Leveraging cloud volume snapshot APIs to image disks out-of-band and analyze file systems without relying on appliance OS access.
- **File Prevalence Analysis:** Exploiting appliance uniformity across deployments to build path and hash baselines, isolating anomalous "long tail" files present on 5% or fewer machines.
- **Real-World Case Studies:** Investigating recent vulnerabilities and uncovering web shells, Sliver C2 implants, and state-sponsored activity across PAN-OS and Ivanti EPMM devices.

### Technical Details
To bypass appliance visibility restrictions, the researchers utilize cloud snapshot APIs to attach appliance disk snapshots to dedicated analysis systems as forensic images. Because appliance file systems are largely identical across deployments, file paths and SHA-1 hashes are aggregated across multiple customer environments to build prevalence histograms:
- **100% Prevalence:** Stock legitimate vendor files.
- **90–100% Prevalence:** Standard files varying due to OS or software versions.
- **10–70% Prevalence:** Common optional add-ons or plugins.
- **<= 5% Prevalence ("The Long Tail"):** High-confidence anomaly zones where malware typically resides.

In the first case study on Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS, attackers chained two vulnerabilities discovered in late 2024 to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. By filtering for low-prevalence files with suspicious extensions (such as PHP) or common files with unique hashes (such as `authorized_keys`), the researchers uncovered multiple web shell instances, including four zero-day malware samples with zero hits on VirusTotal.

In the second case study on Ivanti Endpoint Mobile Manager (EPMM), attackers leveraged a two-vulnerability chain allowing unauthenticated RCE just days after disclosure and public PoC release. By analyzing long-tail SHA-1 hashes linked to unusually large file sizes, the team identified two Sliver C2 framework implants (an open-source Go-based C2), alongside MySQL dumps, reverse shells, and web shells. Pivoting across shared IOCs, malware traits, and DNS history revealed that a single state-sponsored threat actor was responsible for both the PAN-OS and Ivanti campaigns.

### Takeaways
Out-of-band disk snapshot analysis provides scalable forensic visibility into otherwise opaque cloud appliances. However, the speakers noted limitations during Q&A: snapshots cannot detect in-memory/fileless malware and will fail if the appliance disk is encrypted with vendor-managed keys. Defenders without broad cross-tenant data can still apply this technique by taking snapshots and diffing production instances against a clean, stock deployment baseline.

talks.title: whoAMI: Discovering and exploiting a large-scale AMI name confusion attack
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning whoAMI: Discovering and exploiting a large-scale AMI name confusion attack.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Seth Art presents "whoAMI," a research project revealing how AWS EC2 automation workflows (notably Terraform, Go, Python, and shell scripts) can become vulnerable to large-scale AMI name confusion attacks. When automated deployments query Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) using descriptive name filters and dynamic selectors like `most_recent = true` without explicitly specifying an `owners` or `owner-alias` filter, an attacker can publish a public AMI with a matching doppelganger name. Because newly published attacker images have newer timestamps, dynamic resolution selects the malicious image. When the EC2 instance launches, it boots the attacker's image and executes pre-baked command-and-control (C2) payloads, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) and IAM credential compromise in the victim's account.

### Key Topics
- **History of AMI Name Confusion**: Earlier attacks include Haroon Meer and Marco Slaviero's 2009 work brute-forcing low AMI IDs to manipulate ascending sort order in the console, as well as a 2018 HashiCorp Packer finding where omitting `owners` led to Monero miners being fetched (which resulted in a CVE for the AWS CLI). Terraform made `owners` mandatory in 2018, but due to community feature requests in 2022, it became optional again, re-opening the flaw.
- **Prevalence & Attack Surface**: Searching GitHub and Sourcegraph revealed hundreds of vulnerable Terraform repositories, as well as occurrences across Go, Python, and shell scripts. The pattern also impacts delayed executions such as Launch Templates, Auto Scaling groups, and CloudFormation maps.
- **Real-World Impact & Disclosure**: Testing showed between 2% and 4% of customer environments exhibited vulnerable CloudTrail patterns monthly. Coordination with the AWS Vulnerability Disclosure Program revealed two internal non-production AWS systems launching the researcher's benign test AMIs across 70,000 recorded backend events. Testing against Cirrus CI's documented runner setup demonstrated obtaining decrypted secrets (AWS keys, Docker passwords) within runner processes; Cirrus CI resolved the issue within 12 hours.

### Technical Details
- **Exploitation Flow**: The attacker crafts a public AMI mimicking common naming patterns (e.g., Ubuntu or Amazon Linux) with embedded startup C2 agents (such as Sliver or Metasploit). When the victim executes `terraform apply`, dynamic `aws_ami` data source queries resolve the newest match—the attacker's image. At boot, the machine beacons out, granting interactive shell access and any attached EC2 instance profile / IAM permissions (such as S3 bucket access).
- **Detection**: Code can be scanned via Semgrep rules targeting missing owner arguments. At runtime, CloudTrail correlation (e.g., in a SIEM) can identify an `ec2:DescribeImages` call without owner filters followed within 10 minutes by `ec2:RunInstances` by the same principal.
- **HashiCorp AWS Provider Fix**: The provider introduced warnings in version 5.77 and converted missing owner filters combined with `most_recent = true` into a blocking error in version 6.
- **Cloud Image Investigator (`investigator.cloud`)**: The speaker introduced a VirusTotal/URLScan-style investigation platform for AMIs. Leveraging AWS's `source_image_id` and `source_image_region` fields, it maps parent-child lineage back to base images and hashes cloned volume contents to display file-level diffs and anomalous files.

### Takeaways
- **Implement Allowed AMIs**: Use AWS's "Allowed AMIs" feature at the AWS Organizations level via declarative policies for EC2 (starting in audit mode before enforcing blocking mode) to restrict AMI execution to trusted accounts and aliases (`amazon`, `aws-marketplace`).
- **Audit Infrastructure Code**: Explicitly enforce owner filters (`owners = ["amazon"]` or verified account IDs) across all IaC and SDK queries.
- **Enforce Least Privilege**: Restrict IAM roles on EC2 instances using the principle of least privilege, as any instance can become a potential point of initial compromise.

talks.title: Securing Remote MCP Servers
talks.teaser: Explains how to harden remote MCP servers with server-side checks for sessions, OAuth flows and gateways.
talks.summary:
The talk covers the server side of Model Context Protocol (MCP) deployments, since many headline attacks come from client-side tool isolation. The speaker treats local servers as executables that need the usual code scanning, dependency checks and private repositories, and recommends running scans often because these projects change quickly. For remote servers, the speaker discusses streamable HTTP and the older SSE transport, advising origin-header checks against DNS rebinding and avoiding cookie-based authentication to limit CSRF exposure.

Authorization is the central concern. The spec requires OAuth and forbids passing tokens through, yet many implementations put tokens in URLs or forward them downstream, which hampers auditing and rate limiting. Session IDs should be high-entropy, bound to the user and validated on every request, and OAuth flows carry confused-deputy risk around third-party consent screens and dynamic client registration. The speaker favours a platform approach with API gateways so that one well-tested implementation handles tokens and logging.

The closing section covers logging, since agent-driven requests vary more than fixed application calls. Logs should capture tokens, inputs, outputs, user context and both client and server identities. The speaker lists existing FastMCP releases, commercial gateways and open-source gateways as options, and cautions against the original FastMCP 1.0 code. In the Q&A, the speaker said standard API security still applies to the services behind MCP servers.

talks.title: Beyond the Big Three: Mastering Oracle Cloud Security in a Multi-Cloud World
talks.teaser: Shows how to enforce region limits and block public network access in Oracle Cloud using native guardrails.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a product manager at a cloud security startup, explains why customers move workloads to OCI, often because of existing Oracle ties or infrastructure cost, and why they tend to leave the provider's free preventive controls underused. He contrasts OCI's structure with AWS, Azure and GCP, noting that a compartment acts both as a container and as a resource holder, and that policies inherit downward from the root compartment. He also highlights built-in encryption at rest, network separation per customer, granular IAM conditions, and mostly free security services.

The first use case restricts workloads to approved regions for data residency, smaller attack surface and reduced monitoring scope. It can be done with governance rules, which set zero quotas for all resource families and lift them for allowed regions, or with IAM conditions added to each statement. The quota approach has a catch: users can still create some resources, such as object storage, but cannot use them. The second case blocks direct inbound internet access to a sensitive compartment using Security Zones, a CloudGuard feature with built-in policies, and pairs it with a zero quota for public DNS zones to cover managed services.

The talk closes with limitations: one security zone per compartment, no native exclusions, and built-in policies that cannot be customised. Deny statements in IAM had just reached limited availability, and a new simulator was mentioned. The practical takeaway is to combine several native tools instead of relying on one. In the audience Q&A, the speaker said visibility into layered policies exists in his own system and that a simulator is coming.

talks.title: IAM Roles Anywhere - now for everyone with Let's Encrypt
talks.teaser: Shows how to use free Let's Encrypt certificates with AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, plus a TOTP check to detect misuse of stolen keys.
talks.summary:
Workloads outside AWS, such as on-premises servers, GPU providers or legacy Jenkins jobs, often cannot use static keys, OIDC or hardware modules. IAM Roles Anywhere offers a way to assume roles in that situation, but it needs a certificate authority, and public CAs are not accepted as trust anchors. The speaker uses Let's Encrypt's staging intermediate certificates instead, since no browser needs to trust them. Certificates are obtained through ACME with DNS validation, using a cheap domain hosted in Route 53 and a narrowly scoped IAM user with the Lego client. The role's trust policy limits the certificate subject to that domain and its subdomains.

Without an HSM the private key cannot be fully protected, so the speaker binds it to the host instead. A fingerprint of the environment, drawn from files such as /proc and /sys, seeds a time-based one-time password. That six-digit code is sent as the role session name, which the trust policy requires to be exactly six characters. CloudTrail logs the session name, so a script can compare each event with the expected codes and alert on a mismatch. Weekly CRLs are too slow for revocation, so a deny clause on a compromised common name takes effect at once.

The key remains exposed, but misuse becomes detectable. The speaker suggests a 15-minute session duration and monitoring certificate transparency logs for the domain. Six-day Let's Encrypt certificates are planned, which the speaker expects to strengthen the approach.

talks.title: Read Between The Logs: A New Vulnerability in Gemini Cloud Assist Proves the Threat is Real
talks.teaser: Shows how attacker-controlled cloud log entries can inject prompts into Gemini Cloud Assist and lure users into phishing.
talks.summary:
Gemini Cloud Assist is Google Cloud's Gemini integration in the console, used to suggest CLI commands and summarize logs, including through an explain-this-log-entry button. The talk asks what happens when attackers control the content of those logs. The attack begins with an HTTP request to a public cloud function that places instructions in the User-Agent header, which then appears in the resulting log entry.

When a victim clicks the button, the generated prompt includes the full log entry as JSON. Injected special characters break out of that structure so the attacker's text reads as an instruction. The full prompt is hidden behind a details view, so the payload stays out of sight. In the demo, Gemini returned a phishing link presented as more details. The same payload could also be triggered by a user asking Gemini about a broken function. Because Gemini could query resources through the Cloud Asset API, the speaker showed the impact could extend to reading and exfiltrating cloud data via links. Google stopped rendering links, though the speaker noted the prompt injection risk remains.

A comparable test on Azure Copilot did not yield a vulnerability at the time. It could be coaxed into printing a link through its handler parameters, but it could not read the text inside logs. For defenders, the speaker suggested a Log Explorer query that flags prompt-like words such as instruction or markdown in User-Agent headers, and advised treating AI assistants as untrusted, especially if they gain write access.

talks.title: fwd:cloudsec State of the Conference 2025
talks.teaser: Organizers review the conference's budget, speaker mix, sponsors and community efforts, and invite volunteers to step up.
talks.summary:
The organizers give their periodic state-of-the-conference update for Forward CloudSec, a nonprofit-owned, independent event meant to make strong cloud security accessible to everyone. Most of the session is a series of bar charts covering the venue history, talk counts, expenses and income, and sponsor trends. Expenses rose largely because of venue and food costs, and this year speakers received a $600 honorarium. Ticket prices went from $100 to $150, and 11 of 51 sponsors have been acquired, which is 22%.

The speakers flag several concerns. Submitted and accepted talks have levelled off since 2023, and the share of talks from practitioners at companies that are not cloud security vendors has declined, which the honorarium was meant to address. The Slack community keeps gaining members, but many rarely post. The technical oversight committee has taken on the Granted credential tool, so that a single maintainer leaving would not leave it unsupported.

The question-and-answer period covered volunteering, nonprofit finances, venue choice and whether a future event could be held in Canada. The organizers asked attendees to become understudies for sponsorship, logistics and audio-visual work, and to propose new projects they could own. For practitioners, the practical takeaways are to submit talks, mentor scholarship recipients and get involved in the community.
